extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent applicants, district and appellate judges, and pro se parties involved in patent prosecution appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate review of a district-court §145 action challenging PTO/PTAB rejections, focusing on patent-eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101), obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103), and a range of procedural issues (discovery, expert admissibility, amendments, jurisdiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo step one — directed to natural phenomenon or abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept such as a natural phenomenon or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates the 'focus' of the claims to see if they recite subject matter like a product of nature or an abstract idea; example here: claims reciting combinations of nutrients that exist in almonds were found directed to a product of nature. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l, Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo step two — additional limitations must supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims are directed to a natural phenomenon or abstract idea, determine whether additional claim limitations transform the ineligible concept into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional limitations that are 'well-known and conventional' do not supply the requisite inventive concept; merely adding conventional packaging, crushing, administering, selecting, determining, or routine computer components is insufficient. (Cites: Alice; Genetic Techs.; PersonalWeb.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effectively claim a composition or combination that exists in nature are patent-ineligible as a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court compares claimed compositions to naturally occurring substances (example: dosages and components recited are found in almonds); limiting the form (e.g., mixtures or non-specific varieties) does not necessarily avoid a product-of-nature finding if the claimed combination exists in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea — conventional computer implementation does not rescue claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to an abstract idea are not rendered patent-eligible merely by implementing the idea with routine or conventional computer components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim elements that add only conventional computer components or automate an abstract idea (e.g., meal planning) do not transform the claim under Alice step two. (Example: claim 112 found directed to meal planning; adding computer system components was conventional.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlapping dosage ranges in prior art create a presumption of obviousness; challenger must produce evidence of teaching away or unexpected results to overcome the presumption. Court may rely on expert testimony that benefits were well-known in the art to support obviousness. Prior art from the same field of endeavor is particularly persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting obviousness — teaching away and unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut a presumption of obviousness, a patentee may show that prior art taught away from the claimed invention or that the claimed invention produces unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusive assertions are insufficient; the patentee must produce evidence. Failure to show teaching away or unexpected results supports summary judgment of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description / §112 considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. §112 by showing the inventor possessed the claimed invention as described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may reject claims for lack of written description; Board and courts review such rejections on the merits. Procedural default (failure to brief an issue) can lead to summary affirmance on §112 grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness and improper dependency consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can be rejected as indefinite or improperly dependent if claim language fails to provide clear scope or correct dependency structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to present substantive arguments on these grounds on appeal can result in summary affirmance of the rejections; the Board may summarily affirm rejections where appellant does not meaningfully contest them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review — procedural and discovery rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: District court orders on procedure, discovery, complaint amendments, judge recusal, and admissibility of evidence are reviewed for abuse of discretion (appellate review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts afford substantial discretion to district courts in managing discovery and related procedural matters; reversal requires showing an abuse of that discretion. (Cites: Fourth Circuit authorities in opinion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review — dismissals and summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain decisions are reviewed de novo: dismissals under FRCP 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6) and grants of summary judgment (construing evidence in the light most favorable to non-moving party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate court applies de novo review to the legal correctness of dismissals and summary judgment; whether summary judgment was premature is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 56(f) (now Rule 56(d)) — seeking discovery before opposing summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party believes additional discovery is necessary to oppose summary judgment, the proper course is to file a Rule 56(f) (Rule 56(d)) affidavit explaining the need for more discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file such an affidavit is generally sufficient grounds to reject a claim that the opportunity for discovery was inadequate; absent special circumstances (e.g., no opportunity through no fault), summary judgment need not be delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating movant’s facts as undisputed when nonmovant fails to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nonmoving party fails to dispute the movant’s assertions of fact, the court may treat those facts as undisputed for purposes of summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nonmovant must identify specific disputed material facts; generalized or conclusory assertions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daubert admissibility standard — focus on methodology and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to expert testimony under Daubert should address the reliability and relevance of the expert’s principles and methodology, not merely the expert’s conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacks based on alleged mischaracterization of prior art or bias typically go to credibility and weight, not admissibility; courts review Daubert determinations for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert bias/financial interest challenge — weight not admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of an expert’s bias or financial interest generally affect the weight afforded to the testimony rather than its admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disqualification or exclusion for bias is inappropriate where objections concern credibility; cross-examination and competing evidence address weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local procedural rules for pro se filings and motion format
rubrics_metrics.description: Local rules may require pro se parties to submit paper filings rather than use electronic filing, and local rules may require written briefs with motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civ. R. 7(F) and 1(A) and the district’s ECF manual) can require paper motions for pro se litigants; federal rules (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b)(1)(A)) allow courts discretion to grant extensions without motion but do not conflict with local rules that require written motions absent discretionary exception. Courts may waive local requirements in their discretion (E.D. Va. Local Civ. R. 26(B)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusable neglect and good cause for extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain an extension based on excusable neglect or to show good cause after deadlines, a party must show extraordinary circumstances or diligence; mere delay or lack of diligence does not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for 'excusable neglect' only in extraordinary cases where injustice would otherwise result; waiting months after discovery opens or relying on strategic delays is not good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A writ of mandamus is appropriate only where the petitioner shows (1) a clear right to the relief requested and (2) no other adequate remedy is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alternative relief (e.g., §145 suit) exists, mandamus is unavailable; conclusory allegations that an agency must issue a patent do not establish the clear right required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity waiver and jurisdiction for money damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Waivers of sovereign immunity for money damages must be expressed unequivocally by Congress; the Tucker Act grants the Court of Federal Claims exclusive jurisdiction over non-tort money damages claims exceeding $10,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes like 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1338, and 35 U.S.C. §145 do not, absent clear statutory language, waive sovereign immunity for money damages; plaintiffs seeking >$10,000 must generally proceed in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to jury in suits against the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: A Seventh Amendment jury trial right against the United States exists only when Congress, in waiving sovereign immunity, unequivocally provides the right to a jury in the authorizing statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general waiver of sovereign immunity without explicit jury-trial provision does not create a right to jury; courts examine the statute's terms for an unequivocal grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial recusal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Recusal requires showing that a judge has a substantial interest or bias that would tempt an average judge to be biased; adverse rulings alone generally do not establish bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial rulings, critical remarks, or hostile statements ordinarily do not support a successful recusal claim; the movant must show facts establishing a substantial interest or personal bias beyond judicial rulings.
